principle: Whether an additive change is safe is not a property of the wire format — it is conditional on the consumer choosing to be a tolerant reader
because: Every claim in this set that adding a field is 'safe' or 'not breaking' (Graph's catalogue, JSON Schema's open model) is quietly assuming a lenient consumer; the identical change is breaking under a strict/closed-model reader or a real strict-parsing mobile client, so the safety verdict tracks the consumer's leniency, not the change itself.

principle: A Schema Registry compatibility mode is not a validation setting, it is a pre-committed answer to which side — producer or consumer — upgrades first
because: The mode's name, its default, its per-subject override, its transitive variant, and its escape hatch (NONE) all function as one thing: a binding rollout-order commitment, which is why the direction gets inverted so often (A-025) and why a downstream technology like Kafka Streams can still fail even when the mode is technically satisfied (A-014).

principle: Avro resolves schemas by matching field names, and every Avro capability or failure here is a direct consequence of that one choice
because: Aliases exist because name-matching alone cannot distinguish a rename from a delete-plus-add; defaults exist to fill the gap name-matching leaves when a field is genuinely missing; the enum default symbol solves the identical gap for enum values instead of fields; and the trap's asymmetric error behavior (writer-only fields are silently ignored, reader-only fields without defaults error) falls directly out of resolving by name rather than position or number.

principle: Protobuf identifies fields by number on the wire, not by name, and that single fact generates its entire safety discipline
because: Numbers being the actual wire identity is why reuse silently corrupts data instead of erroring, why deletion requires reservation rather than plain removal, why the wire-safe/unsafe tiering exists as a lookup table keyed to that same wire behavior, and why marking a field required creates a one-way commitment no future version can retract; the compare-drill only resolves once a reader can state that Avro matches by name and Protobuf by number.

principle: Where the version identifier lives — URL path, query string, or content-negotiation header — decides what a future change gets coupled to
because: Path versioning couples the version to the URL itself and to gateway routing, so migrating consumers means changing every call site and every co-located service must agree on one mechanism; query-string versioning is only safe once path stability is already guaranteed; header/media-type versioning decouples the version from the URL at the cost of a pastable link — three schemes solving the same problem by choosing a different thing to couple the version to, which is why no scheme is actually free.

principle: Stripe's dated versions, Google's stability channels, and Buf's strictness ladder are the same tradeoff wearing three different names
because: Each replaces a single binary version-surface with a graduated axis specifically to avoid forcing every consumer onto the same all-or-nothing cutover: Stripe trades a growing internal shim chain for consumers who never face a hard migration deadline, AIP's channel/release/visibility axis trades more maintained surfaces for more predictable early-consumer guarantees, and Buf's FILE/PACKAGE/WIRE ladder trades looser enforcement for tolerating renames and file moves — all three answer 'how much internal complexity will we absorb to shrink the version-surface we expose.'

principle: The Deprecation and Sunset headers are a notification layer, and every real deprecation decision happens outside them
because: The headers themselves only carry a date and a link; RFC 8594 says outright that what to do about that date is out of scope, which is exactly the gap that Zalando's consent-and-monitoring process, Azure's review board, and the window-length numbers from Google (180 days) and Microsoft Graph (24-36 months) all fill in — the header signals, but consent, review, and window length are where the actual governance judgment lives.

principle: Consumer-driven contract testing is deliberately narrow, and its value depends on not asking it to be an integration test
because: Pact's own 'test button, not house fire' framing only verifies the specific interaction shape a consumer actually exercises, which is exactly why authorship matters — consumer-driven contracts define what counts as breaking — and exactly why treating passing contract tests as integration coverage is a documented failure mode rather than a hypothetical one; the two workshops drill the identical narrow-scope discipline in different stacks, and the closing drill forces naming the failure class neither test catches.
